extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers, journalists and policymakers interested in the European Investment Bank and EU development/finance
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarise the European Investment Bank's operational rules, priorities, products, governance and policy commitments as described on the Wikipedia article. Useful for research into EIB funding criteria, mandates and instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission and funding scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB is the European Union's investment bank and is owned by the 27 member states. It finances and invests through equity and debt to companies and projects that achieve the policy aims of the European Union and primarily funds projects that 'cannot be entirely financed by the various means available in the individual Member States'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most activity (90%) takes place inside the EU aiming to foster integration; the bank is active in about 140 countries and makes around 10% of investments outside the EU to support EU development aid and cooperation policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lending priorities / thematic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB focuses on the areas of climate, environment, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), development, cohesion and infrastructure (also innovation and skills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects financed should align with one or more EIB priorities. Examples of target areas include renewable energy, energy efficiency, SMEs, digital connectivity, and skills development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green finance commitments and climate alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB is a leading green financier: it was the first institution to issue green bonds (2007), committed in 2019 to stop funding fossil fuel projects by end-2021, pledged to align activities with the Paris Agreement by end-2020, and published the 'Climate Bank Roadmap 2021–2025' including plans to stop funding high-carbon projects and to invest €1 trillion in climate-related projects by 2030.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Roadmap and related policies are the operational commitments that shape project eligibility and sectoral exclusions (e.g., fossil fuels). The Wikipedia article cites these commitments and related timeline milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loan product eligibility and size thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB provides long-term loans, typically up to 50% of a project's overall cost, to public and private sector clients. Private sector direct financing of single large investment projects or programmes typically starts from €25 million; framework loans to public sector entities start from €100 million. Intermediated lending partners channel funds to SMEs up to €12.5 million (below EIB's €25m direct-financing threshold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediated lending allows the EIB to reach smaller borrowers via local banks and partners; lending must be aligned with EIB priorities. Thresholds determine whether EIB finances directly or via intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity investment policy and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB invests and co-invests in companies and funds focused on infrastructure, environment, SMEs and mid-size corporations. Its investments in equity and debt funds usually cover 10% to 20% of the fund size, with a maximum of 25%. It can provide quasi-equity and venture-debt to growth companies and startups in sectors such as biotech, life sciences, software/ICT, engineering and renewables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity/co-investment operations tend to be smaller than traditional EIB deals when aimed at startups; EIF complements the EIB in supporting SMEs and venture activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarantees and credit enhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB provides credit enhancement of senior debt using subordinated financing, funded or unfunded guarantees and contingent credit lines. Guarantees cover a portion of possible losses from a portfolio of loans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit enhancement aims to improve creditworthiness, enhance the protection of senior debt, and help projects attract further private finance. Guarantees are used particularly to support SMEs and mid-caps and to leverage private capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory services: scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Advisory services are carried out by the European Advisory Hub and include strategic and technical guidance on investment mechanisms, market development, financial structuring, procurement, regulation and impact assessment for public and private projects inside and outside the EU.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hub does not offer advice related to the purchase or sale of securities or advisory services regarding project evaluation and audit; advisory services are intended to prepare projects for funding and to improve structuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandates, partnerships and blended finance
rubrics_metrics.description: Apart from financing from its own resources, the EIB establishes mandates and partnerships that help to fund riskier projects and to blend loans with grants; mandates can involve financial investment and technical/financial advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates allow the EIB to operate with partner organisations (e.g., European Commission, UN bodies) and to use blended finance approaches to mobilise additional resources for public-policy objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding model and capitalization (not EU budget-funded)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB is financially autonomous and is not funded through the EU budget; it raises money on international capital markets by issuing bonds. Each member state pays capital into the EIB's reserves broadly in line with their share of EU GDP at accession; subscribed capital figures are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bank's triple-A credit rating (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) allows it to borrow at lower rates and lend at lower rates. Wikipedia includes a detailed subscribed capital breakdown by member state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Green Bond proceeds allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB issues Green Bonds (Climate Awareness Bonds) and with money raised through these bonds the EIB exclusively supports projects that contribute to climate action in renewable energy (wind, hydro, solar, geothermal) and energy efficiency (district heating, co-generation, building insulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EIB was a pioneer in Green Bonds (first in 2007); in 2020 it raised EUR 30.8bn across 16 currencies. Green Bond proceeds are earmarked for defined climate-related disbursements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project appraisal: viability and carbon emissions screening
rubrics_metrics.description: Project financing is granted after preliminary screenings of the project's viability and the carbon emissions associated with the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screenings form part of EIB's internal appraisal and are used to determine alignment with investment priorities and climate/ESG policies (e.g., under the Investment Plan for Europe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic eligibility and regional focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB is active in some 140 countries grouped into regions (Enlargement countries, EFTA, EU Southern Neighbourhood, EU Eastern Neighbourhood, Sub-Saharan Africa, Caribbean and Pacific, Asia and Latin America, Central Asia and the United Kingdom). Approximately 90% of activity is inside the EU and about 10% outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside-EU investments are intended to support EU development aid and cooperation policies; geographical groupings and mandates guide where the EIB operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: EIF mandate and SME support
rubrics_metrics.description: The European Investment Fund (EIF), part of the EIB Group, is the EU's venture capital arm that supports SMEs across all stages (pre-seed, seed, start-up, growth) and provides guarantees for SMEs. The EIF typically co-invests or guarantees via partner financial intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EIB is the EIF's majority shareholder (62%); EIF works with banks, guarantee, leasing and microfinance institutions, private equity and venture capital funds to reach SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis response financing mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB plays a role in crisis financing (examples: 2008 financial crisis, COVID-19) by providing dedicated instruments such as the Pan-European Guarantee Fund (EGF) approved May 2020, intended to mobilise up to €200 billion and support companies affected by the pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EGF eligibility: European Union companies are eligible if they have financial issues due to the pandemic but could have secured loans under pre-crisis circumstances. The EIB also provided direct loans to companies engaged in vaccine development and manufacturing (e.g., BioNTech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, governance, oversight and complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB Group has published policies such as the EIB Group Transparency Policy, Environmental and Social Standards, Anti-Fraud Policy and a Complaints Mechanism Policy; it is subject to oversight and scrutiny by bodies including the European Parliament, European Court of Auditors and the European Anti-Fraud Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia notes criticisms and controversies (insufficient stakeholder consultation, lack of transparency, alleged staff harassment) and references the public register, complaints mechanism and corporate governance reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and Social Standards (operational policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The EIB has Environmental and Social Standards (referenced as a 2018 policy) that set requirements and expectations for projects it finances with respect to environmental and social performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These standards are part of project appraisal and compliance; related policies include transparency and anti-fraud provisions and are publicly available on EIB.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shareholder capital subscription principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Each EU member state is subscribed in capital based on its economic weight (expressed in GDP) within the EU at the time of accession; following the UK's withdrawal remaining member states proportionally increased capital subscriptions to maintain overall subscribed capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wikipedia includes a detailed table with paid-in capital, uncalled capital and total subscribed capital by member state, illustrating the capital structure and changes after events like Brexit.
